2: The memory of the appalling catastrophe that in August 1883 struck the island of Krakatoa and the neighbouring coasts of Java and Sumatra
3: is—as always happens—effaced by the stream of later events and impressions.
4: Yet we may well suppose that it has not vanished altogether,
5: or the readers of our periodical will peruse with interest the following account by Mr Edmond Cotteau, who, by order of the French government,
6: a few months after the disaster visited the regions ravaged by the eruption and reported what he found.
7: Of the eruption itself none of those still living were witnesses; yet from the destruction it wrought

9: We now give the floor to Mr Cotteau.
10: On 11 May 1884 I found myself, after a very interesting excursion to Sarawak (Borneo), at Singapore.
11: The Oxus, of the Compagnie des Messageries Maritimes, had just arrived; on board were my two friends,
12: Messrs Bréon and Korthals, with whom, on behalf of the Ministry of Public Instruction,
13: a scientific mission to the Sunda Strait and the volcanic island of Krakatoa had been entrusted.
14: I had left Paris a month earlier: we now met again at the appointed place.
15: On the evening of the same day we went aboard the steamer
16: which, twice a month after the arrival of the French mail, carries passengers and letters to Batavia,
17: where we arrived on 14 May, after a pleasant voyage of fifty-two hours.
18: As soon as we were comfortably settled, we took the steps necessary to ensure the success of the mission entrusted to us,
19: which could not be accomplished without help and cooperation from higher authority.
21: The Consul of France, Count de Pourtalès, was eager to serve us;
22: the Governor-General of the Dutch Indies, Mr van der Put, and the Director of the Royal Observatory at Batavia, Mr van Bemmelen,
23: placed themselves entirely at our disposal.
